content: UCP3, or mitochondrial uncoupling protein 3, is a protein encoded by the UCP3 gene in humans. It belongs to the family of mitochondrial anion carrier proteins, which play a critical role in separating oxidative phosphorylation from ATP synthesis. This process dissipates energy as heat, a phenomenon often referred to as mitochondrial proton leak. UCP3 is specifically involved in the transfer of anions from the inner mitochondrial membrane to the outer mitochondrial membrane, as well as the reverse transfer of protons. This mechanism is thought to protect mitochondria from oxidative stress. Uncoupling proteins, including UCP3, reduce the mitochondrial membrane potential in mammalian cells. While UCP1 is primarily expressed in brown adipocytes, UCP2 is more widely distributed across tissues. The exact mechanism by which UCPs transfer H+ or OH− ions remains unclear. UCP3, in particular, is considered an important mediator of thermogenesis, contributing to the regulation of body temperature and energy expenditure. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) associated with UCP3, such as rs1800849, rs11235972, rs1726745, and rs3781907, have been identified. Studies in different populations have shown a correlation between the -55CT mutation in UCP3 and lower body mass index (BMI). This relationship appears to be influenced by energy intake, suggesting a complex interaction between genetic factors, diet, and metabolic outcomes. Variability in prior studies may reflect these interactions. Structurally, UCPs contain three homologous protein domains characteristic of mitochondrial anion carrier proteins (MACPs). The UCP3 gene exhibits tissue-specific transcription initiation, with additional transcription initiation sites upstream of the major skeletal muscle site (SM-1). The chromosomal arrangement of UCP3 is 5'-UCP3-UCP2-3', and two splice variants of the gene have been identified. Mutations in the UCP3 gene are associated with obesity and metabolic disorders. For example, a mutation in exon 3 (V102I) has been identified in an individual with obesity and diabetes. Similarly, a stop codon mutation in exon 4 (R143X) and a splice donor mutation in exon 6 were found in a compound heterozygote with severe obesity and diabetes. The allele frequencies of these mutations were similar in African American and Mende populations but absent in Caucasians. Heterozygosity for the exon 6 splice donor mutation was associated with a 50% reduction in fat oxidation rates, highlighting a role for UCP3 in metabolic fuel partitioning. UCP3 has also been implicated in hypoxia resistance in renal epithelial cells and is upregulated in renal cell carcinoma. The -55CT polymorphism of UCP3 has been linked to body weight regulation and energy consumption in type 2 diabetic patients. As an inhibitor, UCP3 influences long-chain fatty acid metabolism and prevents cytosolic triglyceride storage. Additionally, UCP3 has been shown to interact with the protein YWHAQ, further underscoring its involvement in complex cellular processes.
